claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles is governed by a buffering anion sublattice such as an engineered surface oxide.
A buffering oxide layer limits atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles.
A buffering oxide layer limits phase segregation.
A buffering oxide layer preserves a single-phase, near-equiatomic solid solution at high temperature.
The starting nanoparticles have a uniform metal distribution.
The starting nanoparticles possess a thin, naturally or intentionally formed oxide layer.
A controlled oxidation treatment can be used to establish a pre-formed buffering oxide layer.
Inert-atmosphere synthesis and handling will maintain a minimal or absent oxide layer in the control nanoparticles.
Catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K constitute relevant high-temperature service regimes.
The buffering oxide sublayer stabilizes local chemical order.
The oxide sublattice acts as both a physical and chemical barrier to metal-atom diffusion.
Suppression of metal-atom diffusion causes reduced phase segregation and elemental redistribution.
Reduced diffusion maintains the single-phase solid solution during thermal and chemical stress.
Oxide-coated nanoparticles will retain phase homogeneity better than nanoparticles lacking the controlled oxide layer.
Oxide-coated nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than nanoparticles lacking the controlled oxide layer.
Oxide-coated nanoparticles will provide superior catalytic performance relative to nanoparticles lacking the oxide layer.
Oxide-coated nanoparticles will provide superior thermoelectric performance relative to nanoparticles lacking the oxide layer.
Nanoparticles without intentional oxide formation will undergo greater phase degradation and elemental segregation under identical service conditions.
The stabilization effect should be significant when an anion sublattice is inherent or can be engineered.
The oxide-mediated stabilization effect may be diminished in strictly inert environments or in systems where oxide formation is energetically unfavorable.
